cmo-cmo-1999-01.title: Fix the integer part
cmo-cmo-1999-01.body:
Let $n = [x]$. The equation says $40n = 4x^2 + 51 > 0$, so $n \ge 1$, hence $x \ge 1 > 0$ and
$$x = \frac{\sqrt{40n - 51}}{2}.$$
This $x$ is a solution exactly when its integer part really is $n$, i.e. $n \le x < n + 1$, i.e.
$$4n^2 \le 40n - 51 < 4(n+1)^2.$$
- Left inequality: $4n^2 - 40n + 51 \le 0 \iff (2n - 3)(2n - 17) \le 0 \iff \frac32 \le n \le \frac{17}{2}$, so $n \in \{2, 3, \ldots, 8\}$.
- Right inequality: $4n^2 - 32n + 55 > 0 \iff (2n - 5)(2n - 11) > 0 \iff n < \frac52$ or $n > \frac{11}2$.

Together: $n \in \{2, 6, 7, 8\}$, giving
$$x = \frac{\sqrt{29}}{2} \approx 2.69,\quad \frac{\sqrt{189}}{2} \approx 6.87,\quad \frac{\sqrt{229}}{2} \approx 7.57,\quad \frac{\sqrt{269}}{2} \approx 8.20,$$
and each indeed has integer part $2, 6, 7, 8$ respectively (e.g. $16 < 29 < 36$ gives $2 < \frac{\sqrt{29}}2 < 3$).

**Answer: $x \in \left\{\frac{\sqrt{29}}{2}, \frac{\sqrt{189}}{2}, \frac{\sqrt{229}}{2}, \frac{\sqrt{269}}{2}\right\}$**

cmo-cmo-1999-01.title: Bound x first
cmo-cmo-1999-01.body:
From $x - 1 < [x] \le x$:
- $4x^2 + 51 = 40[x] \le 40x$ gives $(2x - 3)(2x - 17) \le 0$, i.e. $\frac32 \le x \le \frac{17}2$;
- $4x^2 + 51 = 40[x] > 40x - 40$ gives $(2x - 7)(2x - 13) > 0$, i.e. $x < \frac72$ or $x > \frac{13}2$.

So $[x] \in \{1, 2, 3\}$ or $[x] \in \{6, 7, 8\}$. Try each value $n$ of $[x]$ with $x = \frac{\sqrt{40n - 51}}{2}$: $n = 1$ gives $4x^2 = -11$, impossible; $n = 3$ gives $x = \frac{\sqrt{69}}2 > 4$, wrong integer part; $n = 2, 6, 7, 8$ give $\frac{\sqrt{29}}2, \frac{\sqrt{189}}2, \frac{\sqrt{229}}2, \frac{\sqrt{269}}2$, which have the right integer parts.

**Answer: $\frac{\sqrt{29}}{2}, \frac{\sqrt{189}}{2}, \frac{\sqrt{229}}{2}, \frac{\sqrt{269}}{2}$**

cmo-cmo-1999-02.title: Coordinates: the chord has length 1
cmo-cmo-1999-02.body:
**Set-up.** The circle touches line $AB$ and has its centre $O$ on the same side as $C$, at distance $1$ from $AB$ — the same distance as $C$. So $O$ lies on the line through $C$ parallel to $AB$. Place $C = (0, 0)$ with $AB$ on the line $y = 1$: $A = (\frac1{\sqrt3}, 1)$, $B = (-\frac1{\sqrt3}, 1)$, and $O = (a, 0)$. "Rolling along the segment $AB$" means the point of tangency $(a, 1)$ is on $AB$: $|a| \le \frac1{\sqrt3}$. The circle is $(x - a)^2 + y^2 = 1$; the triangle is $\{0 \le y \le 1,\ |x| \le \frac{y}{\sqrt3}\}$, i.e. the part of the angle $\angle ACB$ below $y = 1$.

**Where the sides cut the circle.** The ray $CA$ consists of the points $t\,(\frac12, \frac{\sqrt3}{2})$, $t \ge 0$. Substituting into the circle: $t^2 - at + a^2 - 1 = 0$. The product of the roots is $a^2 - 1 < 0$, so there is exactly one positive root $t_A$: the ray $CA$ meets the circle exactly once, at $A'$. Similarly the ray $CB$ (direction $(-\frac12, \frac{\sqrt3}2)$) gives $t^2 + at + a^2 - 1 = 0$ with exactly one positive root $t_B$, at $B'$. Every point of the circle has $y \le 1$, so $A'$, $B'$ lie on the sides $CA$, $CB$.

**The arc inside.** $C$ is inside the circle ($|CO| = |a| < 1$), so each ray from $C$ meets the circle exactly once; the rays inside $\angle ACB$ sweep out exactly one arc from $A'$ to $B'$, and these points have $y \le 1$, so this arc is precisely the part of the circle inside the triangle. It lies in the half-plane $y \ge 0$, i.e. within a semicircle of the circle (centre on $y = 0$), so its central angle is at most $180^\circ$.

**Its length.** In triangle $A'CB'$ the angle at $C$ is $60^\circ$, so
$$A'B'^2 = t_A^2 + t_B^2 - t_At_B = (t_A + t_B)^2 - 3t_At_B.$$
From the quadratics, $t_A = \frac{a + \sqrt{4 - 3a^2}}{2}$, $t_B = \frac{-a + \sqrt{4 - 3a^2}}{2}$, so $t_A + t_B = \sqrt{4 - 3a^2}$ and $t_At_B = \frac{(4 - 3a^2) - a^2}{4} = 1 - a^2$. Hence
$$A'B'^2 = 4 - 3a^2 - 3 + 3a^2 = 1.$$
So $OA' = OB' = A'B' = 1$: triangle $OA'B'$ is equilateral and the arc (central angle $\le 180^\circ$) has central angle $60^\circ$. Its length is $1\cdot\frac{\pi}{3} = \frac\pi3$, independent of the position $a$. ∎

cmo-cmo-1999-02.title: Synthetic: an inscribed angle of 30°
cmo-cmo-1999-02.body:
As in the first approach, the centre $O$ lies on the line $\ell$ through $C$ parallel to $AB$, $C$ is inside the circle, and the arc inside the triangle runs from $A'$ (on side $CA$) to $D$ (on side $CB$), lying on the side of $\ell$ containing $AB$.

Since $\ell \parallel AB$, the lines $CA$ and $CB$ make angles of $60^\circ$ and $120^\circ$ with $\ell$ (measured in the same rotational sense), so the reflection in $\ell$ maps line $CB$ onto line $CA$; it fixes $C$ and maps the circle to itself (its centre is on $\ell$). Hence it maps $D$ to the point $E$ where the extension of $AC$ beyond $C$ meets the circle, and $CE = CD$.

Triangle $CED$ is isosceles with apex angle $\angle ECD = 180^\circ - \angle ACB = 120^\circ$, so $\angle CED = 30^\circ$. Since $E$, $C$, $A'$ are collinear with $C$ between them, $\angle A'ED = 30^\circ$. This is an inscribed angle on the arc $A'D$ not containing $E$ — the arc inside the triangle ($E$ is on the other side of $\ell$). So that arc has central angle $60^\circ$ and length $\frac\pi3$ for every position of the circle. ∎

cmo-cmo-1999-03.title: Odd squares and the bound p^t ≥ 2t + 1
cmo-cmo-1999-03.body:
$n = 1$ works ($d(1) = 1$). Let $n > 1$ with $n = d(n)^2$.

**$n$ is an odd square.** $n$ is a perfect square, so $n = p_1^{2\beta_1}\cdots p_m^{2\beta_m}$ with distinct primes $p_i$ and $\beta_i \ge 1$. Then $d(n) = (2\beta_1 + 1)\cdots(2\beta_m + 1)$ is odd, so $n = d(n)^2$ is odd: all $p_i \ge 3$. Taking square roots, the condition becomes
$$p_1^{\beta_1}p_2^{\beta_2}\cdots p_m^{\beta_m} = (2\beta_1 + 1)(2\beta_2 + 1)\cdots(2\beta_m + 1). \tag{1}$$

**Lemma.** For a prime $p \ge 3$ and an integer $t \ge 1$, $p^t \ge 2t + 1$, with equality only for $p = 3$, $t = 1$.

*Proof.* For $t = 1$: $p \ge 3$, equality iff $p = 3$. If $p^t \ge 2t + 1$, then $p^{t+1} \ge 3p^t \ge 3(2t + 1) > 2t + 3$, so the inequality is strict for all $t \ge 2$. $\square$

By the lemma each factor on the left of (1) is at least the matching factor on the right, so (1) holds only if every factor gives equality: $p_i = 3$ and $\beta_i = 1$ for all $i$. As the primes are distinct, $m = 1$ and $n = 3^2 = 9$. Indeed $d(9) = 3$ and $3^2 = 9$.

**Answer: $n = 1$ and $n = 9$**

cmo-cmo-1999-04.title: Add up thirteen differences
cmo-cmo-1999-04.body:
Relabel so that $a_1 < a_2 < \cdots < a_8$. Suppose, for contradiction, that no positive difference $a_i - a_j$ occurs three or more times.

Consider the $7 + 6 = 13$ differences
$$d_i = a_{i+1} - a_i\ (1 \le i \le 7), \qquad e_i = a_{i+2} - a_i\ (1 \le i \le 6).$$
They come from $13$ different pairs $(i, j)$, so by assumption each value occurs among them at most twice. Their sum is
$$\sum d_i + \sum e_i = (a_8 - a_1) + (a_7 + a_8 - a_1 - a_2) = 2(a_8 - a_1) + (a_7 - a_2) \le 2(17 - 1) + (16 - 2) = 46,$$
using $a_8 \le 17$, $a_1 \ge 1$, $a_7 \le 16$, $a_2 \ge 2$.

On the other hand, $13$ positive integers in which no value appears more than twice have sum at least
$$2(1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6) + 7 = 49 > 46.$$
Contradiction. So some $k > 0$ occurs as $a_i - a_j$ for at least three different pairs. ∎

**Example with seven numbers:** $\{1, 2, 4, 7, 11, 16, 17\}$. Its $21$ positive differences are
$$1, 3, 6, 10, 15, 16;\ \ 2, 5, 9, 14, 15;\ \ 3, 7, 12, 13;\ \ 4, 9, 10;\ \ 5, 6;\ \ 1$$
(differences from $1, 2, 4, 7, 11, 16$ to the larger elements), and each value appears at most twice. (Many other sets work.)

cmo-cmo-1999-05.title: Push z to 0, then AM–GM
cmo-cmo-1999-05.body:
Let $f(x, y, z) = x^2y + y^2z + z^2x$. It is unchanged by the cyclic shift $(x, y, z) \to (y, z, x)$, so we may assume $x = \max(x, y, z)$.

**Step 1: reduce to $x \ge y \ge z$.** A direct expansion gives
$$f(x, y, z) - f(x, z, y) = (x - y)(y - z)(x - z).$$
If $x \ge z \ge y$, this is $\le 0$, so $f(x, y, z) \le f(x, z, y)$, and $(x, z, y)$ is ordered as first $\ge$ second $\ge$ third. So it suffices to bound $f$ when $x \ge y \ge z$.

**Step 2: move $z$ into $x$.** For $x \ge y \ge z \ge 0$,
$$f(x + z, y, 0) - f(x, y, z) = (x + z)^2y - x^2y - y^2z - z^2x = z^2y + yz(x - y) + xz(y - z) \ge 0.$$

**Step 3: AM–GM.** With $u = x + z$, $u + y = 1$:
$$f(u, y, 0) = u^2y = 4\cdot\frac u2\cdot\frac u2\cdot y \le 4\left(\frac{\frac u2 + \frac u2 + y}{3}\right)^3 = \frac{4}{27}.$$
So $f \le \frac{4}{27}$ always.

**Equality.** In the case $x \ge y \ge z$: Step 3 needs $\frac u2 = y$, i.e. $y = \frac13$, $x + z = \frac23$; Step 2 needs $z^2y + yz(x-y) + xz(y-z) = 0$, and with $y > 0$ the term $z^2y$ forces $z = 0$. So $(x, y, z) = (\frac23, \frac13, 0)$. In the case $x \ge z > y$ we would need equality for $(x, z, y)$, i.e. $(x, z, y) = (\frac23, \frac13, 0)$, but then $f(x, y, z) = f(\frac23, 0, \frac13) = \frac2{27} < \frac4{27}$. Undoing the cyclic shift, equality holds exactly at
$$(x, y, z) = \left(\tfrac23, \tfrac13, 0\right),\ \left(0, \tfrac23, \tfrac13\right),\ \left(\tfrac13, 0, \tfrac23\right).$$
∎
